extracted.intended_audience: patent owners, patent prosecutors, and patent litigators (counsel preparing patents and complaints and defending against §101 motions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patents and complaints and litigating to survive Rule 12(b)(6) motions asserting patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, with practical steps for pleadings, specification drafting, venue selection, and use of evidence/declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step Alice §101 framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the two-step framework: (1) determine whether the claim, as a whole, is directed to patent-ineligible subject matter (e.g., an abstract idea or law of nature); (2) if so, consider whether the claim contains an inventive concept sufficient to 'transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that this framework contains underlying factual questions; courts will resolve these questions when evaluating eligibility. Use this framework as the baseline legal test when evaluating claims and drafting pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading standard for §101 at Rule 12(b)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rule 12(b)(6), facts in the complaint are taken as true with all reasonable inferences drawn for the nonmoving party, but the court need not accept legal conclusions couched as factual allegations or allegations that contradict the face of the patent, exhibits, or matters subject to judicial notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plead facts must be plausible, specific, and sufficiently concrete for an action to survive a §101 motion. Courts may dismiss when no factual allegations, accepted as true, prevent resolving §101 as a matter of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conclusory or boilerplate allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that are merely boilerplate or conclusory (e.g., attorney argument that the claims provide new computer functionality) are insufficient to survive a §101 motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on attorney argument to create factual disputes. Courts have rejected boilerplate assertions that claims 'do not merely recite computers carrying out business practices' where such statements contradict the patent language or specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should recite technological improvements (not generic computer use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should recite an improvement to the computer or technology itself and not merely use a computer or other conventional technology as a tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to make inventive features evident in claim language — e.g., implementation of a particular machine or a particular way of programming software to achieve the invention — so that particular improvements can be clearly alleged in a complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft specification to describe technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe in the specification how the invention is a technological improvement over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not strictly required if claims and complaint sufficiently allege improvements, a detailed specification may make it more difficult for defendants to prevail at the pleadings stage by providing support for nonabstract, inventive features (e.g., figures and tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Align complaint allegations with patent claims and specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations in the complaint must not be wholly divorced from the patent claims and the specification; they should align with the patent's plain language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach the patent as an exhibit to the complaint so allegations can be directly supported by the specification (including figures/tables). Inconsistent allegations (e.g., claiming technical details not reflected in the claims/spec) risk dismissal with prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert declarations to create fact issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach an expert declaration when necessary to bolster alleged improvements, but the declaration must clearly define the inventive aspect and demonstrate, nonconclusorily, where nonabstract technological improvements are found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have relied on nonconclusory expert declarations at the pleadings stage to find fact disputes. Beware: conclusory expert statements that merely assert unconventionality without support have been rejected and can lead to dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible extrinsic evidence and judicial notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners may rely on extrinsic evidence subject to judicial notice, such as the patent's prosecution history and general historical observations, when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts will take judicial notice of well-known, general historical observations and similar background facts in resolving eligibility questions at the pleadings stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether claim limitations are routine or conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: In high‑tech cases, courts will consider whether claim limitations, alone or in combination, demonstrate well‑understood, routine, or conventional activity, and whether the method is implemented with generic computing technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and pleadings to show that limitations are not routine/conventional and to explain how the claimed application improves the capability of the system as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show that claimed functions improve system capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that a proposed new application or computer‑implemented function is an improvement to the capability of the system as a whole (not merely an abstract idea implemented on generic hardware).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, describe how the invention improves performance, functionality, or other technological attributes of the computer/system, and capture those improvements in both claims and specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue selection as litigation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider filing in venues that are less inclined to grant §101 Rule 12(b)(6) motions; venue choice can materially affect success rates at the pleadings stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article notes the Eastern District of Texas has historically been more favorable to patent owners than courts such as the Northern District of California and the District of Delaware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contradictions between complaint and patent/exhibits
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not plead allegations that contradict the face of the patent, exhibits to the complaint, or matters subject to judicial notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will ignore allegations that contradict the patent and may dismiss claims where the complaint's assertions are inconsistent with the patent's plain language; ensure consistency to avoid dismissal with prejudice after amendment opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand impact of Federal Circuit decisions raising factual issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that decisions like Berkheimer and Aatrix emphasize that eligibility determinations can involve subsidiary factual questions, which may preclude resolution on the pleadings if disputes exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the potential for factual disputes to argue that §101 cannot be decided as a matter of law at the pleadings stage when supported by concrete allegations or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to allege concrete improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the complaint provides no support beyond tying generic allegations to an abstract idea, the patent owner risks dismissal (potentially with prejudice), especially after multiple amendment opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure initial complaints are concrete and specific; repeated failures to provide nonconclusory allegations can lead to dismissal with prejudice.
